newsitem.title: USA: Jewish group calls for Swiss probe of Nazi accounts.
newsitem.headline: Jewish group calls for Swiss probe of Nazi accounts.

text.p: A Jewish group on Sunday called for Switzerland to investigate all secret bank accounts opened by Nazi officials during the Third Reich and turn over the money to Holocaust victims.

The Simon Wiesenthal Centre, based in Los Angeles, made public a letter to Swiss President Arnold Koller urging the Swiss government and banks to turn over any assets in the accounts to a fund established to compensate Nazi victims.

Rabbi Marvin Hier, founder of the Wiesenthal Centre, said he sent a list of 334 prominent Nazi officials, bankers and industrialists most likely to have transferred looted assets to Switzerland between 1933 and 1945.
"We plan to send a similar request to other neutral countries like Spain and Argentina," Hier told Reuters in a telephone interview.

He cited declassified U.S. intelligence documents from 1945 as saying that high Nazi officials sought a safe haven from the crumbling Reich and shipped large stores of gold, jewels and foreign securities across the Swiss border.

Only a small amount of gold has ever been recovered, Hier said, and Switzerland has "never been pressured into giving a full accounting of their banks' relationships with the leaders of the Third Reich" because of Swiss bank secrecy laws.
Hier said officials on the list were "these so-called elite" who were able to open accounts and move money and goods across borders because of their rank and connections to Nazi leaders.

"We even included the names of their wives, mistresses and aliases which could have been used to open accounts," Hier said. "Swiss banks keep records extremely well so this should not be difficult to research."

Among the names on the list were Gestapo chief Heinrich Muellar, Alois Brunner, who was also known as Dr. Georg Fisher and is alleged to live now in Syria, and Max Amann, Adolph Hitler's top business adviser.

The list also included directors of concentration camps, doctors who performed experiments on prisoners, police bosses and others like Hitler's artwork adviser, Karl Haberstock, alleged to have plundered valuable paintings from destroyed Jews that have never surfaced in public.

Jewish groups were outraged last year when Swiss economy minister and then rotating president Jean-Pascal Delamuraz said the country was being blackmailed by world Jewish leaders into setting up a fund to compensate Holocaust victims.
He later apologised and the Swiss government has moved to start such a fund.

In New York last Friday, some major participants in the dispute publicly declared an end to a bitter confrontation at a meeting among Jewish leaders and Swiss, Israeli and U.S. officials. It ended with participants hailing a new spirit of cooperation to resolve what has been called the last chapter of the Holocaust -- a battle over how to compensate victims.
Jewish organisations had been considering calling for a boycott by Jews around the world of Swiss banks.

"Things are back on track after getting out of hand and emotional," World Jewish Congress President Edgar Bronfman said, at a news conference in which he was flanked by the chief U.S. and Swiss officials dealing with the issue.

The Swiss government, which six weeks ago said it would never establish such a fund, announced last week that it would take over a private $71 million fund set up by the country's three biggest banks and work with the WJC and Swiss Jews to set up a mechanism for its "timely distribution."
